nodes.label: Inline assistant use
nodes.one_line: Use an inline AI coding assistant — completion, inline edit — inside the editor for single-file changes.
know_what: Inline completion — ghost-text suggestions as you type (Copilot, Cursor Tab), accepted or dismissed per keystroke, the lightest-weight form of AI assistance
Inline edit — selecting a block of code and asking for a targeted rewrite in place, distinct from a full chat conversation
Suggestion acceptance rate as a signal — noticing how often you're rejecting suggestions, which says something about whether the tool is tuned to the codebase's conventions
Latency-accuracy tradeoff — inline tools optimize for speed over the deeper reasoning a chat-based session can do, appropriate for small, local edits, not larger changes
Autocomplete vs intent — an inline suggestion completing what's typically written next versus what this specific task actually needs, a gap worth noticing
know_how: Accept an inline suggestion only after reading it, not by reflex
Reject a suggestion that pattern-matches to something generic rather than the actual local context
Use inline edit for small, local, mechanical changes and switch to a chat session for anything needing broader context
Notice repeated wrong suggestions in one area as a signal the assistant lacks context there, not just bad luck
Keep an eye on suggestions for the same near-miss pattern (off-by-one, wrong variable) to catch it before it becomes a habit of quick acceptance
habits: Read every inline suggestion before accepting it, especially longer ones
Switch to a chat-based tool once an inline edit starts needing more than one file of context
Notice and mentally flag any suggestion that seems to ignore visible local conventions
Slow down acceptance speed on unfamiliar files compared to ones you know well
Treat a string of rejected suggestions in a row as a cue to add more context rather than keep tabbing through
nodes.checkpoint: Given an editor with inline AI completion enabled, write a small function while correctly accepting useful suggestions and rejecting at least one plausible-looking but subtly wrong one.
nodes.common_failure: Accepting inline suggestions by reflex because they're fast and usually right — the rare wrong one (a swapped argument order, a slightly wrong comparison) slips through exactly because acceptance became automatic rather than reviewed.

nodes.label: Chat-to-code loop
nodes.one_line: Run the basic chat loop: describe a change, receive a diff or file, apply it, check the result.
know_what: Chat-to-code loop — describe, receive, apply, check: the basic cycle of any chat-based coding assistant interaction
Apply step — the moment a proposed diff or file actually gets written to disk, distinct from the assistant merely describing what it would do
Copy-paste vs tool-integrated apply — manually moving code from a chat window versus a tool that applies a diff directly, with different risks of transcription error
Turn-by-turn verification — checking the result after each turn of the loop rather than running several turns unchecked and reviewing at the end
Loop termination — recognizing when the loop has actually converged on a correct result versus when it's cycling without making real progress
know_how: Describe one change, apply it, and check the result before describing the next change
Verify the applied result matches what was actually proposed, not just trust the apply step worked
Check for a wrong or partial apply (a diff that didn't fully land) before continuing the loop
Recognize loop stagnation — repeated turns with no real progress — and stop rather than continuing indefinitely
Keep each turn's ask narrow enough that checking its result is fast
habits: Check the result after every single turn, not after a batch of several
Confirm an applied diff actually landed as described before building on it
Stop the loop and reassess once two turns in a row haven't made real progress
Keep asks in the loop small enough to verify quickly, splitting a big ask into turns
Treat a loop where each turn expands scope instead of narrowing it as a sign to stop and re-decompose
nodes.checkpoint: Run a five-turn chat-to-code loop implementing a small feature, verifying the applied result after each turn, and correctly recognize and stop a sixth turn that would just repeat a prior failed attempt.
nodes.common_failure: Running several turns of the loop back to back without checking in between, so a bad apply in turn two silently becomes the foundation every later turn builds on, and the error isn't caught until a much bigger review at the end.

nodes.label: Multi-file agent tasks
nodes.one_line: Direct an agentic coding tool to make a coordinated change across multiple files in a single task.
know_what: Multi-file agent task — a single instruction that results in coordinated edits across several files, requiring the agent to maintain consistency between them
Cross-file consistency — a rename, type change, or interface update correctly propagated to every caller, not just the file where it was defined
Task scope for multi-file changes — naming which files are in scope up front, since an agent's search for 'everywhere this needs to change' can over- or under-reach
Partial application risk — a multi-file change landing correctly in some files but not others, leaving the codebase in an inconsistent, non-compiling state
Search-then-edit pattern — an agent finding every relevant location before editing, versus editing opportunistically as it encounters references, with different risk of missing a spot
know_how: State the scope of a multi-file change explicitly (which files, which callers) before letting an agent search freely
Run a build or type check immediately after a multi-file change to catch any file that wasn't updated consistently
Ask the agent to list every file it identified as needing a change before it starts editing, so omissions are visible up front
Review every touched file in a multi-file diff, not just the one that was the nominal target
Grep for the old pattern after a rename or interface change to confirm nothing was missed
habits: Run a full build or type check immediately after any multi-file agent change
Search for the old identifier or pattern after a rename to confirm the change was complete
Read the list of touched files before the diff content, checking it matches expectations
Treat a multi-file change that touches fewer files than expected as a signal something was missed, not a pleasant surprise
Confirm the touched-file count roughly matches a manual grep of where the old pattern actually appeared
nodes.checkpoint: Given an interface used in 6 files, direct an agent to change its shape and confirm all 6 call sites were updated consistently by running a full type check afterward.
nodes.common_failure: Trusting an agent's own claim that a rename or interface change is complete — a multi-file task can miss a caller in a file the agent didn't think to search, and the gap only surfaces later as a type error or runtime failure in an unrelated part of the app.
sources: software engineering writing on large-scale refactors

nodes.label: Tool permission scoping
nodes.one_line: Configure what an agent may do unattended — read-only, edit, run commands — and set that scope deliberately per task.
know_what: Permission scope — the explicit set of actions an agent is allowed to take unattended (read-only, file edit, command execution, network access), configured per task rather than granted globally
Read-only mode — an agent that can inspect and propose changes but not apply them, useful for exploration or a first pass before granting write access
Allowlist vs denylist — permitting specific known-safe commands versus blocking specific known-dangerous ones, with different failure modes when a new, unlisted case appears
Scope-per-task vs scope-per-session — granting broad permissions once for a whole session versus re-scoping for each distinct task within it, a real tradeoff between friction and safety
Elevated-risk actions — file deletion, force-push, package installation, and similar actions that warrant a narrower default scope than routine file edits
know_how: Set an agent's permission scope deliberately before starting a task, rather than accepting whatever the tool defaults to
Use read-only or plan-only mode for exploration or a first pass on an unfamiliar area before granting write access
Narrow the scope for any task involving deletion, force operations, or installing new dependencies
Re-evaluate scope per task rather than leaving a broad grant in place indefinitely out of convenience
Check what scope was actually granted after configuring it, rather than assuming the configuration took effect as intended
habits: Default to the narrowest scope that lets a task get done, widening only when a concrete need appears
Treat any request for command-execution or network scope with more scrutiny than a request for file-edit scope
Re-check granted scope before starting a new, different task rather than assuming yesterday's scope still fits
Note which scope a task actually needed after finishing it, to calibrate the next similar task's default
Revoke or narrow a broad grant once the task that needed it is finished, rather than leaving it standing
nodes.checkpoint: Given a task that only requires reading and proposing changes, configure an agent's permission scope to read-only/propose-only, and verify it cannot apply an edit without further explicit approval.
nodes.common_failure: Granting broad edit-and-execute permissions by default because narrowing them per task feels like friction — the cost of that convenience shows up the one time a task goes sideways and the agent had more reach than the task actually needed.

nodes.label: Command execution review
nodes.one_line: Review a shell command an agent proposes before letting it run, especially anything destructive or network-facing.
know_what: Proposed command — a shell command an agent wants to run, which should be read and understood before approval just like a code diff
Destructive command class — deletion, force-push, database drops, and similar commands whose effects are hard or impossible to undo, warranting a higher bar of scrutiny
Network-facing command — a command that sends data externally (curl to an unfamiliar host, a package install from an unusual source), worth checking the destination and payload of
Command intent vs command effect — what a command is meant to do versus what it will actually do, which can diverge with a subtly wrong flag or argument
Approval fatigue — the tendency to rubber-stamp command approvals after many uneventful ones in a row, exactly when a dangerous one is most likely to slip through
know_how: Read a proposed command's full text, including flags, before approving it, not just its general shape
Look up an unfamiliar flag or command before approving it rather than assuming it's safe because the rest of the command looks routine
Check the target of any network-facing command (the URL, the host) explicitly
Pause longer on any command in the destructive class (rm, drop, force-push) than on a routine read or build command
Notice and counteract approval fatigue by re-reading commands carefully even after many safe approvals in a row
habits: Read every proposed command in full before approving, regardless of how many safe ones preceded it
Treat any destructive or network-facing command as worth extra scrutiny by default
Look up unfamiliar flags rather than assuming they're benign
Notice when approvals are starting to feel automatic and deliberately slow back down
Keep a mental or written list of command patterns that always deserve a second look (rm, force-push, drop, curl to a new host)
nodes.checkpoint: Given a sequence of ten proposed commands, nine routine and one a disguised destructive command (e.g. rm -rf with a wildcard), correctly identify and block the destructive one before it runs.
nodes.common_failure: Approving commands quickly after a long streak of safe ones, exactly the condition under which a genuinely dangerous command is most likely to be waved through without being read carefully.
sources: software engineering writing on automation approval fatigue

nodes.label: Custom agent instructions
nodes.one_line: Write persistent project instructions — a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md-style file — that steer every future agent session's defaults.
know_what: Standing instructions file — a file (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursorrules) an agent reads automatically at the start of every session, setting defaults without re-stating them each time
Project conventions as instructions — naming, testing, and structural conventions written down once so every future session follows them without being told per prompt
Instruction scope — what belongs in a standing file (durable, cross-session conventions) versus what belongs in a one-off prompt (task-specific detail)
Instruction drift — a standing instructions file going stale as the project's actual conventions evolve, producing agent output that follows outdated guidance
Instruction precedence — how a standing instruction interacts with a conflicting one-off prompt instruction, and which should win (usually the more specific, current one)
know_how: Write down a convention in the standing instructions file the second time it has to be repeated in a prompt, not the fifth
Keep the instructions file scoped to durable, cross-session facts, not task-specific detail that belongs in a single prompt
Review and update the instructions file when project conventions actually change, not just when writing it the first time
Test that a fresh session actually follows a new instruction before assuming it's absorbed
Keep the file short enough to be read and internalized, not a dumping ground for everything ever said
habits: Add a new convention to the standing file the moment it's had to be repeated across sessions
Periodically re-read the instructions file for anything that's now stale or contradicted by current code
Verify a new instruction actually changes agent behavior in a fresh session before trusting it's working
Keep the file organized enough that a specific convention can be found quickly, not buried in an undifferentiated list
Remove an instruction from the file once it no longer reflects how the project actually works
nodes.checkpoint: Given a convention that's had to be manually restated in three separate sessions, add it to the standing instructions file and confirm a fresh session follows it without being told again.
nodes.common_failure: Letting the instructions file grow into an unmaintained dumping ground of every past correction, most of them stale — a bloated, contradictory instructions file gets followed less reliably than a short, current one, defeating its purpose.

nodes.label: Autonomous task delegation
nodes.one_line: Hand a bounded multi-step task to an agent to run unattended, with a clear definition of done and a way to check the result.
know_what: Bounded task — a task with a clear start, a clear definition of done, and a clear scope, the specific shape suitable for unattended agent delegation
Definition of done — the concrete, checkable condition that tells you (and the agent) the task is actually finished, stated before delegation, not inferred afterward
Unattended run — an agent working through a multi-step task without a human approving each individual step, relying instead on its configured permission scope and its own judgment
Result verification vs process trust — checking the actual outcome of a delegated task against its definition of done, rather than trusting that the agent's own summary of what it did is accurate

Delegation failure modes — a task that was too loosely bounded (agent goes off in an unintended direction) versus one that was too tightly scoped (agent gets stuck unable to complete it), both signals for how to write the next delegation
know_how: Write a clear definition of done before delegating a task, not after the agent has already started
Scope the task narrowly enough that 'done' is unambiguous, splitting an ambiguous task into bounded pieces first
Check the actual result against the definition of done after the run, not just read the agent's self-report
Review the diff and any side effects (files created, commands run) of an unattended run in full before accepting it
Note whether a delegated task went off-track due to scope or due to an unclear definition of done, to calibrate the next delegation
habits: Write the definition of done before delegating, every time, even for a task that feels obvious
Verify a completed delegated task against its actual result, not against the agent's summary of the result
Review the full diff and command history of an unattended run before accepting it
Treat an agent's self-reported 'done' as a claim to check, not a fact
Delegate a smaller, more tightly bounded version of a task after a run that went off-track, rather than repeating the same loose delegation

know_why.claim: A delegated task's definition of done should be written before the agent starts, not inferred from what it produces.
know_why.because: Without a definition fixed in advance, 'done' silently becomes whatever the agent produced, and a plausible-looking result gets accepted even when it diverges from what was actually needed — the same confirmation-bias risk as grading your own exam after seeing the answer.
know_why.disputed_by: The vibe-loop school argues that for exploratory tasks, the definition of done genuinely isn't knowable until you've seen a first attempt, and prefers delegating loosely and refining scope based on what comes back.
know_why.source: Anthropic — building effective agents; practitioner writing on agent task delegation

nodes.checkpoint: Write a definition of done for a bounded multi-step task, delegate it to an agent to run unattended, and correctly judge whether the result satisfies the definition — not just whether the agent claims success.
nodes.common_failure: Delegating a task with only a vague goal and no definition of done, then accepting whatever the agent produces because it looks plausible and the agent reports success — without a concrete bar, there's no way to distinguish a correct result from a confident-looking wrong one.
sources: practitioner writing on autonomous coding agents

nodes.label: Multi-agent coordination
nodes.one_line: Run multiple agents on independent parts of a codebase in parallel without their changes stepping on each other.
know_what: Parallel agent run — multiple agents working simultaneously on different parts of a codebase, each with its own session and context
Partition boundary — the division of work (by directory, by module, by feature) chosen so parallel agents' changes don't overlap or conflict
Merge conflict at the task level — two agents both needing to touch the same shared file, the specific risk that makes partition choice the central design decision of parallel delegation
Shared-state hazard — a file, config, or interface that multiple parallel tasks depend on, needing either to be excluded from all of them or explicitly coordinated

Coordination overhead — the real cost (defining partitions, reviewing more surface area at once, resolving any overlap) that has to be smaller than the time saved by running in parallel for it to be worth it
know_how: Partition work along real module or directory boundaries before starting parallel agents, not by arbitrary task count
Identify shared files or interfaces up front and exclude them from parallel tasks, or handle them in a separate, sequential step
Review each parallel agent's diff separately before merging, rather than reviewing the combined result as one undifferentiated blob
Run each parallel task on its own branch so a conflict, if one occurs, surfaces as a normal git merge conflict rather than silent overwrite
Compare the actual time saved against the coordination overhead honestly, since parallelizing a task with heavy shared state can cost more than it saves
habits: Choose partition boundaries before launching parallel agents, never split work arbitrarily after the fact
Check for a shared file or interface touched by more than one parallel task before merging
Review each agent's branch independently before combining, not just the final merged diff
Reconsider parallelizing the next similar task if this one's coordination overhead exceeded its time savings
Default to sequential delegation unless a partition is genuinely obvious, rather than parallelizing by default

know_why.claim: Parallel agents are only worth the coordination overhead when the work partitions along real, independent boundaries.
know_why.because: The cost of running agents in parallel isn't the agent time, it's the human cost of defining non-overlapping partitions and reviewing multiple simultaneous diffs; when the work doesn't actually decompose cleanly, that overhead exceeds whatever time parallel execution saved.
know_why.disputed_by: Some agentic-autonomy practitioners argue that with good tooling (automatic conflict detection, isolated worktrees), the partitioning overhead is small enough that defaulting to parallel agents for any multi-part task is still a net win, even when boundaries are imperfect.
know_why.source: Practitioner writing on multi-agent coding workflows (Anthropic's agentic coding guidance; community writeups on parallel agent orchestration)

nodes.checkpoint: Given a task naturally split across two independent modules, run two agents in parallel on separate branches with no shared-file overlap, and merge both without a conflict.
nodes.common_failure: Splitting a task into 'parallel' pieces that both need to touch the same shared config or interface file — the agents don't coordinate with each other, so one's change silently overwrites or conflicts with the other's, and the time saved by parallelizing is lost resolving the collision.
sources: community writeups on multi-agent coding orchestration
